newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil opposition says CPI probe still on track.
newsitem.headline: Brazil opposition says CPI probe still on track.

text.p: Brazil's opposition parties will petition Congress' lower house Tuesday to form a wide-ranging investigative panel to probe an alleged cash-for-votes scheme rocking Brasilia despite last-minute government moves to scuttle the attempt.

Deputy Jose Machado, the leader of the Workers Party (PT) in the Chamber of Deputies, told Reuters Friday the opposition still has the signatures needed to force the lower house to create the special investigative panel, known by its Portuguese acronym as a CPI.
The bid to form the panel was tripped up late Thursday when 19 pro-government lawmakers withdrew their names minutes before the session ended, leaving the opposition short on signatures.
But Machado said the PT by early Friday had garnered another 40 names.
"We have approximately 200 names and we only need 171," Machado said, adding the petition will be presented Tuesday at the next full session of the lower house.
He added the PT and other opposition parties would continue gathering names to move the CPI to a top-priority spot on the agenda.
With 171 signatures, the petition for a CPI moves automatically to the bottom of the line of other probes requested in the lower house.
However, if the opposition is able to gather 257 signatures, it could ensure a vote on a motion to move its CPI to the top of the line and have an investigative panel formed immediately.
At present, there are five other CPIs in progress, the maximum allowed in Brazil's lower house. With only 171 signatures, there is no telling when this CPI would come on the agenda.

Although the oppositon may be able to force the creation of a lower house panel, it is unlikely it will be able to muster the 27 Senate signatures needed to form a full congressional CPI. The Senate is more conservative than the fractious lower house.
The government and Congress have been rocked this week by allegations five deputies took bribes to vote in favor of a bill allowing President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to stand for re-election.

Reports in Folha de Sao Paulo also linked Communications Minister Sergio Motta to the cash-for-votes scheme, suggesting he may have provided some of the money as well as a television station in Brazil's far-western state of Acre.
Motta has denied the allegations and Cardoso has dismissed them as baseless "insinuations."
